all_historical_figures.name: Frithjob Schuon
all_historical_figures.significance: His expressions 'luminous obscurity' and 'obscured light' are used to describe the dual nature of the temple's symbol (manifestation and content).

all_historical_figures.name: Aśoka
all_historical_figures.significance: The practice of building stūpas gained enormous importance during his reign. The architectural form finalized in his days survived in later stūpas.
all_historical_figures.dates: Reigned c. 268 – c. 232 BCE (Implied by context)

all_historical_figures.name: Mahendravarman I
all_historical_figures.significance: An inscription claims he was the innovator of rock-cut shrines built without traditional materials like brick or timber. He was a versatile patron of arts and author, known by titles 'Vicitra-citta' and 'Cheṭṭakāri'.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāravi
all_historical_figures.significance: Patronized by King Mahendravarman I.

all_historical_figures.name: Appar
all_historical_figures.significance: Influenced King Mahendravarman I, who subsequently built many shrines to Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Narasimhavarman I
all_historical_figures.role: Pallava King, successor to Mahendravarman I
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the world-famous monolithic shrines ('Rathas') at Māmallapuram. Bore the title 'Māmalla'.

all_historical_figures.name: Tvaṣṭr
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the fashioner of divine habitations in old Indian texts of architecture.

all_historical_figures.name: Guṇaśīla
all_historical_figures.significance: Patron of the cave-temple at Nāmakkaḷ, dedicated to Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Kīrtivarman I
all_historical_figures.significance: Patron of the earliest and largest cave-temple (No. 111) at Bādāmi, dedicated to Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Maṅgaḷīśa
all_historical_figures.significance: Co-ruler during the excavation of the Bādāmi cave-temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Mṛgeśa-varman
all_historical_figures.significance: The Jina temple at Halasi dates back to his reign.

all_historical_figures.name: Dāmodara-varman
all_historical_figures.significance: Probable builder of the Chejerla shrine, originally a Buddhist sanctuary.
all_historical_figures.dates: First few centuries of the Christian era

all_historical_figures.name: Ptolemy
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned the town of Paṭṭadakallu in his writings.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa I
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Kailāsa temple at Ellorā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikramāditya II
all_historical_figures.significance: King associated with the Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakallu.

all_historical_figures.name: Loka-mahādevī
all_historical_figures.role: Queen of Cāḷukya King Vikramāditya II
all_historical_figures.significance: The Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakallu may have been named Lokeśvara after her.

all_historical_figures.name: Anivārita-guṇḍa
all_historical_figures.significance: Named in an inscription as the architect of the Paṭṭadakallu temple, a rare instance of a craftsmaster being given recognition.

all_historical_figures.name: Vijayāditya
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Vijayeśvara (Saṅgameśvara) temple at Paṭṭadakallu.

all_historical_figures.name: Percy Brown
all_historical_figures.significance: His opinion is cited regarding the dedication of the Pāpanātha temple to Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Baladevamayya
all_historical_figures.significance: His name is inscribed on the Naṭarāja panel in the Pāpanātha temple at Paṭṭadakallu.

all_historical_figures.name: Narasimhavarman II (Rājasimha)
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Shore-temple at Māmallapuram and the Kailāśanātha temple at Kāñcīpuram, key examples of the Drāviḍa style.

all_historical_figures.name: Heliodorus
all_historical_figures.significance: A devotee of Viṣṇu who erected a stone column (garuḍa-dhvaja) at Besnagar, indicating the existence of a temple.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājūvala
all_historical_figures.significance: An inscription states he built a stone temple for the five heroes of the Vṛṣṇi clan in Mora, near Mathurā.

all_historical_figures.name: Shoḍāśa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the inscription of his father.

all_historical_figures.name: Ānanda Coomaraswamy
all_historical_figures.significance: Assigned the famous Śiva icon from Guḍimallam to the first century B.C.

all_historical_figures.name: Prajāvāti
all_historical_figures.significance: Gifted an inscribed sculpture of a four-armed Viṣṇu in the village of Burhikhār.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājarāja I
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Rājarājiśvara (Bṛhadeśvara) temple at Tāñjāvūr.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājendra-Coḷa
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the temple at Gaṅgaikoṇḍa-colapuram.

all_historical_figures.name: Sāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: His interpretation of the word 'vimāna' is cited in the context of its symbolism.

all_historical_figures.name: Marihi
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as the author of the Ānanda-saṃhitā, which classifies worship into bodily, verbal, and mental types.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for his denunciation of a learned brahmin who teaches sacred texts for pay as a 'hireling' (bhṛtakādhyāpaka), highlighting the orthodox prejudice against professional priests.

all_historical_figures.name: Aparārka
all_historical_figures.significance: A Smṛti ascribed to him is quoted, which states that an icon ('pratimā') is for people of little intelligence, representing the orthodox viewpoint.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhārad-vāja-nṛsiṃha
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as the author of the Arcanā-tilaka.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhrgu
all_historical_figures.significance: Quoted within the Arcanā-tilaka, distinguishing between worship 'with external props' (sālamba) and 'without them' (nirālamba).

all_historical_figures.name: Kubera-Vaiśravaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the 'overlord of the lords' from whom earthly kings derive their glory, and who himself attends on God, justifying the royal treatment of the deity in a temple.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as receiving the ancestral conch from the ocean of milk. Said to be represented in the conch.

all_historical_figures.name: Rudra
all_historical_figures.significance: Represented by clarified butter (ghṛta) in the pañcagavya mixture.

all_historical_figures.name: Soma
all_historical_figures.significance: Represented by curds (dadhi) in the pañcagavya mixture.

all_historical_figures.name: Śukra
all_historical_figures.significance: Represented by milk (kṣīra) in the pañcagavya mixture.

all_historical_figures.name: Naṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Represented by cow's urine (go-mūtra) in the pañcagavya mixture.

all_historical_figures.name: Arka or Sun
all_historical_figures.significance: Represented by cow's refuse (go-maya) in the pañcagavya mixture.

all_historical_figures.name: Varuṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Said to abide in the middle portion of the conch.

all_historical_figures.name: Prajāpati
all_historical_figures.significance: Said to reside in the tail portion of the conch.

all_historical_figures.name: Gangā and Sarasvati
all_historical_figures.significance: Said to reside in the front portion of the conch.

all_historical_figures.name: Hanumān, Garuḍa, Nandi or Cakra
all_historical_figures.significance: Their forms adorn the handle of the ritual bell (ghaṇṭā), signifying the vital principle (prāṇa-śakti).

all_historical_figures.name: Brahma
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the deity for whom sandal-paste (gandha) is a favourite article of offering.

all_historical_figures.name: Vāmana
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked in curds during the pañcāmṛta-snāna ritual.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked in ghee during the pañcāmṛta-snāna ritual. Also mentioned as one of the five forms conjured up by the worshipper (Satya, Puruśa, Acyuta, Aniruddha and Viṣṇu).

all_historical_figures.name: Madhūsudana
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked in honey during the pañcāmṛta-snāna ritual.

all_historical_figures.name: Acyuta
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked in sugar during the pañcāmṛta-snāna ritual. Also mentioned as one of the five forms conjured by the worshipper.

all_historical_figures.name: Govinda
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked in milk during the pañcāmṛta-snāna ritual.

all_historical_figures.name: Indra
all_historical_figures.significance: His victory over the demon Vṛtra is cited as the mythological origin of festivals on earth. His figure is also painted on festival flags.

all_historical_figures.name: Vṛtra
all_historical_figures.significance: His defeat by Indra was celebrated by the gods, creating the model for all mortal festivals.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: A text (Śrī-praśna) states he gave Indra the strength and guidance to defeat Vṛtra. His carrier, Garuḍa, is used as a festival emblem and vehicle. Nine-day festivals are said to please him.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.role: Chief of the gods / Creator God
all_historical_figures.significance: The most important temple festival, 'brahmotsava', is named after him as he is believed to personally conduct it. One-day festivals are said to please him.

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: His vehicle, the bull Vṛśabha, is used on festival flags and as a vehicle. Three-day festivals are said to please him.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣmī
all_historical_figures.significance: Seven-day festivals are said to please her.

complete_timeline.event: Consecration of the Rājarājiśvara (Bṛhadeśvara) temple at Tāñjāvūr.
complete_timeline.significance: A high point of Coḷa architecture, featuring a towering vimāna.

complete_timeline.event: Building of the temple at Gaṅgaikoṇḍa-colapuram.
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the trend towards shorter vimānas compared to the Tāñjāvūr temple.

complete_timeline.event: Rule of the Guptas.
complete_timeline.significance: A period of great temple-building in North India, during which the śikhara evolved.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Pallava King Mahendravarman I.
complete_timeline.significance: Pioneering period for rock-cut shrines in the Pallava kingdom.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Pallava King Narasimhavarman I.
complete_timeline.significance: Creation of the monolithic 'rathas' at Māmallapuram.

complete_timeline.event: Building of the Kailāsa temple at Ellorā by Kṛṣṇa I.
complete_timeline.significance: A monumental rock-cut temple, possibly inspired by the Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakallu.

complete_timeline.event: Vedic culture
complete_timeline.significance: A cultural period where fire (Agni) was the primary object of worship, and icon worship was likely not popular.

complete_timeline.event: Erection of Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar.
complete_timeline.significance: Early epigraphic evidence of Viṣṇu worship and temple existence, with Indo-Greek influence.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of stūpas at Bārhut, Bodhgayā, Sārnāth and Sānci.
complete_timeline.date: First and the third centuries B.C.
complete_timeline.significance: Represents the Buddhist adaptation of the stūpa form, which became massive hemispherical structures.

complete_timeline.event: Dating of the Guḍimallam Śiva icon by Coomaraswamy.
complete_timeline.significance: Indicates that free-standing icons are older than many structural temples.

complete_timeline.event: Churning of the ocean of milk
complete_timeline.significance: The ancestral conch is said to have emerged during this event, establishing its divine origin.

complete_timeline.event: Defeat of the demon Vṛtra by Indra
complete_timeline.significance: The celebration of this victory by the gods is presented as the origin and model for all festivals in the mortal world.

complete_timeline.event: Rise of Tāntrik ideology
complete_timeline.significance: Introduced and popularized the worship of divinity in human/semi-human forms (mūrti), diagrams (maṇḍala), and the use of mantras, leading to the prominence of temples and icons.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of Parasurāmeśvara temple at Guḍimallam.
complete_timeline.significance: An early structural temple in South India, housing a significant early icon of Śiva.

complete_timeline.event: Ghosuṇḍi inscription mentioning a stone temple-enclosure for Vāsudeva and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
complete_timeline.significance: Early evidence for the Bhāgavata cult and temple structures in Rajasthan.

complete_timeline.event: Excavation of caves at Junnār.
complete_timeline.significance: Example of early rock-cut architecture, functioning as retreats for monks.

complete_timeline.event: Excavation of caves at Kṛṣṇagiri or Kanheri.
complete_timeline.significance: Part of the wave of excavated cave architecture in Western India.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Kadamba ruler Mṛgeśa-varman.
complete_timeline.significance: Date associated with the Jina temple at Halasi.

complete_timeline.event: Excavation of caves at Ellorā.
complete_timeline.significance: A major site of rock-cut architecture featuring Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain caves.

complete_timeline.event: Excavation of cave No. 111 at Bādāmi.
complete_timeline.significance: The earliest and largest of the Bādāmi cave-temples.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II (Rājasimha).
complete_timeline.significance: Construction of the Shore Temple and Kailāśanātha temple, defining the Drāviḍa style.

complete_timeline.event: Ptolemy mentions Paṭṭadakallu.
complete_timeline.significance: Early mention of a key temple site by a foreign traveller.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of Durgā temple at Aihole began.
complete_timeline.significance: An important early structural temple in the Karṇāṭaka region, showing adaptation of Buddhist chaitya details.

complete_timeline.event: Building of the Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakallu.
complete_timeline.significance: A major temple likely modeled on the Rājasimha temple at Kāñcīpuram.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of Paraśurāmeśvara temple at Bhuvaneśvar.
complete_timeline.significance: Illustrates the transition of the Nāgara idiom to the North, showing links to the Durgā temple at Aihole.

complete_timeline.event: Rule of King Guṇaśīla.
complete_timeline.significance: Period of the Nāmakkaḷ cave-temples in Tamil Nadu.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of Lād-Khān temple at Aihole.
complete_timeline.significance: An early structural stone-temple in Karṇāṭaka, preceding the cave-temples.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of Pāpanātha temple at Paṭṭadakallu.
complete_timeline.significance: An early temple at the site showing North Indian features and disregard for canonical proportions.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of temples at Khajurāho.
complete_timeline.significance: Development of a variant Nāgara idiom in Central India with a focus on sculptural enthusiasm.

all_geographic_locations.context: Archaeological remains show evidence of domestic shrines but no public temples.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Supports the theory that domestic shrines predate public temples.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sites of major Buddhist stūpas built between the 1st and 3rd centuries B.C.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Prime examples of the architectural form of the stūpa finalized in Aśoka's time.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of 150 excavated caves from around 100 A.D.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of early, extensive rock-cut cave complexes.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of eight excavated caves from around 150-189 A.D.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Another example of early Western Indian rock-cut architecture.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of about 27 excavated caves, mostly from the first few centuries after Christ.
all_geographic_locations.significance: World-famous for its rock-cut caves and murals.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of about 33 excavated caves (c. 550-750 A.D.), including the Kailāsa temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major site demonstrating the pinnacle of rock-cut architecture.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of an inscription of Mahendravarman I claiming to have built a rock-cut shrine.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Key evidence for the Pallava innovation in temple construction.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sites of stone temples that were several centuries earlier than Mahendravarman I's rock-cut shrines.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Challenges the claim that Mahendravarman I was the first to conceive of stone temples.

all_geographic_locations.context: Locations of numerous temples ascribed to Mahendravarman I.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the extent of temple-building activity under his patronage.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the world-famous monolithic 'Rathas' and the Shore Temple, built by Pallava kings.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A crucial site for the development of the Drāviḍa style of architecture.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of two excavated cave-temples dedicated to Viṣṇu from around 750 A.D.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows Pallava-era influence in a different region.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of four important Cāḷukya cave-temples from the 6th century.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A center for the Cāḷukyas where a fusion of stylistic details occurred.

all_geographic_locations.context: A 'temple-town' with over 70 temples, including early structural ones like Lād-Khān and Durgā temples.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows great antiquity of structural temples in the Karṇāṭaka region.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Parasurāmeśvara temple (2nd century A.D.) with a very early Śiva icon.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the oldest monumental temple experiments in South India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Kapotīśvara shrine (4th century), originally a Buddhist sanctuary.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important early structural temple whose apsidal form influenced later rock-cut shrines.

all_geographic_locations.context: An important Cāḷukya township with about ten ancient temples, including the famous Virūpākṣa temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A 'crucible' where different temple styles (Nāgara, Drāviḍa) were experimented with, marking a transition from rock-cut to structural forms.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Paraśurāmeśvara, Mukteśvara, and Liṅgarāja temples.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the development of the Orissan style of Nāgara architecture over several centuries.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of about twenty extant temples built between 950-1050 A.D.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Represents a variant idiom of Central Indian temple architecture, known for its sculptural richness.

all_geographic_locations.context: City where the Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus resided.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A center of Indo-Greek culture and influence.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the Heliodorus pillar.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Early site of a Bhāgavata cult temple.

all_geographic_locations.context: Near the site of Mora, where Rājūvala built a stone temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important center of religious activity in ancient North India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of a 2nd century B.C. inscription mentioning a temple enclosure.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Early evidence of temple structures in Western India.

all_geographic_locations.context: The icon here was originally free-standing according to early Āḻvār songs.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An example of an icon predating its temple structure.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the Bṛhadeśvara temple built by Rājarāja I.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A masterpiece of Coḷa architecture and the Drāviḍa style.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a major temple built by Rājendra-Coḷa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Demonstrates the evolution of Coḷa architecture after the Tāñjāvūr temple.

all_geographic_locations.context: The Raṅganātha temple here has seven enclosing walls.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An extreme example of a massive temple complex encompassing a whole township.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as a region where the hold of the 'āgamas' is perceived to be stronger in temples.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Contrast with North India to discuss the reach and uniformity of Āgamic influence.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as a region where temples also follow 'āgamas', though they may be less numerous or widely known than in the South.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Used to argue that the differences in temple worship between North and South are more superficial than real.

all_geographic_locations.context: Listed as an example of a celebrated temple in the North where 'āgamas' play a very significant role.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Evidence for the prevalence of Āgamic procedures beyond South India.

all_geographic_locations.significance: Evidence for the prevalence of Āgamic procedures beyond South India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Listed as an example of a celebrated temple in the North, and later as a temple whose history illustrates its importance in the evolution of the population's ethos.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key site of Āgamic worship and an example of a temple's deep historical and cultural impact.

all_geographic_locations.context: Cited as an example of a temple where the daily worship in the sanctum remains strictly unaltered despite numerous festivals, which are conducted outside. Also mentioned for having a very large number of festivals (429 per year in the 17th century).

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned in the context of specific musical instruments used during temple festivals.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Indicates a regional focus for the specific cultural practices described.
